prompt: Carbon uses two kinds of orbitals, 2s and 2p, for bonding. What does experiment show about the four C–H bonds in methane?

choices.text: All four are identical, pointing toward the corners of a regular tetrahedron
One C–H bond differs from the other three
choices.why: That is what you might expect from one 2s and three 2p orbitals, but in fact all four bonds are identical.

choices.text: Two are made from 2s orbitals and two from 2p orbitals
choices.why: Carbon's valence orbitals are one 2s and three 2p, and in any case the four bonds turn out to be identical.

choices.text: They all lie in one plane at 90° to each other
choices.why: The bonds point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, with 109.5° angles.

explanation: We might expect methane to have two kinds of C–H bonds, but all four are identical and spatially oriented toward the corners of a regular tetrahedron. Hybridization explains this.

prompt: Who showed in 1931 how an s orbital and three p orbitals can combine to form four equivalent tetrahedral orbitals?

choices.text: Linus Pauling
G. N. Lewis
choices.why: Lewis proposed the shared-electron covalent bond in 1916.

choices.text: August Kekulé
choices.why: Kekulé proposed that carbon is tetravalent (1858) and forms rings (1865).

choices.text: Jacobus van 't Hoff
choices.why: Van 't Hoff proposed the tetrahedral carbon in 1874, but the hybrid-orbital explanation came from Pauling.

explanation: In 1931 Linus Pauling showed mathematically how an s orbital and three p orbitals on an atom can combine, or hybridize, to form four equivalent atomic orbitals with tetrahedral orientation.

prompt: Which atomic orbitals combine to form sp3 hybrid orbitals?

choices.text: One s orbital and three p orbitals
Three s orbitals and one p orbital
choices.why: The superscript 3 refers to p orbitals: one s plus three p.

choices.text: One s orbital and two p orbitals
choices.why: That combination gives sp2 hybrids (Section 1.8).

choices.text: One s orbital and one p orbital
choices.why: That combination gives sp hybrids (Section 1.9).

explanation: An s orbital and three p orbitals combine, or hybridize, to form four sp3 hybrid orbitals oriented toward the corners of a regular tetrahedron.

prompt: How many sp3 hybrid orbitals does a carbon atom form?
explanation: Combining one 2s and three 2p orbitals gives four equivalent sp3 hybrid orbitals, one for each of carbon's four bonds.

prompt: What does the superscript 3 in sp3 tell you?

choices.text: That three p orbitals combine with one s orbital to form the hybrid
That the hybrid orbital holds three electrons
choices.why: The superscript tells how many of each type of orbital combine, not how many electrons occupy it.

choices.text: That the hybrid orbitals are in the third shell
choices.why: Carbon's sp3 hybrids are made from its second-shell (2s and 2p) orbitals.

choices.text: That three hybrid orbitals are formed
choices.why: Four sp3 hybrids are formed, from four atomic orbitals.

explanation: The superscript 3 in sp3 tells how many of each type of atomic orbital combine to form the hybrid (one s, three p), not how many electrons occupy it.

prompt: Why do sp3 hybrid orbitals form stronger bonds than unhybridized s or p orbitals?

choices.text: One lobe is larger than the other, so it overlaps more effectively with another atom's orbital
They hold more electrons
choices.why: Every orbital holds at most two electrons; the difference is the shape.

choices.text: They are spherical, so they overlap in every direction
choices.why: sp3 hybrids are unsymmetrical, with one large lobe pointing in one direction.

choices.text: They are lower in energy than any atomic orbital
choices.why: The book's explanation is about shape: a larger lobe gives better overlap.

explanation: sp3 hybrid orbitals are unsymmetrical about the nucleus. One of the two lobes is larger than the other and can therefore overlap more effectively with an orbital from another atom, so sp3 hybrids form stronger bonds.

prompt: Why are sp3 hybrid orbitals unsymmetrical about the nucleus?

choices.text: The positive p lobe adds to the s orbital while the negative p lobe subtracts from it
The nucleus is off-center in the atom
choices.why: The asymmetry comes from combining the s and p wave functions, not from the nucleus.

choices.text: Each sp3 orbital holds one electron on one side
choices.why: Electron occupancy doesn't set the shape; the signs of the p lobes do.

choices.text: The s orbital is larger than the p orbital
choices.why: The difference comes from the opposite algebraic signs of the two p lobes.

explanation: The two lobes of a p orbital have different algebraic signs, + and −. When a p orbital hybridizes with an s orbital, the positive p lobe adds to the s orbital but the negative p lobe subtracts from it, so the hybrid is strongly oriented in one direction.

prompt: What is the H–C–H bond angle in methane, in degrees?
explanation: The four sp3 hybrid orbitals point to the corners of a regular tetrahedron, so each H–C–H angle is 109.5°, the tetrahedral angle.

prompt: What is the length of a C–H bond in methane, in picometers?
explanation: Each C–H bond in methane has a length of 109 pm and a strength of 439 kJ/mol.

prompt: What is the strength of a C–H bond in methane, in kJ/mol?
explanation: Each C–H bond in methane has a strength of 439 kJ/mol (105 kcal/mol).

prompt: A C–H bond in methane has a strength of 439 kJ/mol. What is that in kcal/mol? (1 kJ = 0.2390 kcal)
explanation: 439 kJ/mol × 0.2390 kcal/kJ = 104.9 kcal/mol, which the book rounds to 105 kcal/mol.

prompt: What is the shape of a methane molecule?

choices.text: Tetrahedral, with carbon at the center
Flat and square, with 90° bond angles
choices.why: The four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron, with 109.5° angles.

choices.text: Trigonal planar
choices.why: That is the shape around an sp2 carbon (Section 1.8). Methane's carbon is sp3.

choices.text: Linear
choices.why: Linear geometry goes with sp carbons, as in acetylene (Section 1.9).

explanation: Each of carbon's four sp3 hybrids overlaps a hydrogen 1s orbital, giving four identical C–H bonds pointing to the corners of a regular tetrahedron, with 109.5° angles between them.

prompt: Which orbitals overlap to form each C–H bond in methane?

choices.text: A carbon sp3 hybrid orbital and a hydrogen 1s orbital
A carbon 2p orbital and a hydrogen 1s orbital
choices.why: If carbon used unhybridized orbitals, its bonds wouldn't all be identical; it uses sp3 hybrids.

choices.text: A carbon 2s orbital and a hydrogen 1s orbital
choices.why: Carbon's 2s orbital is mixed into the four sp3 hybrids, which form the bonds.

choices.text: Two sp3 hybrid orbitals
choices.why: Hydrogen has only its 1s orbital; sp3–sp3 overlap is how two carbons bond (Section 1.7).

explanation: When each of the four identical sp3 hybrid orbitals of carbon overlaps with the 1s orbital of a hydrogen atom, four identical C–H bonds are formed and methane results.

prompt: Hybridization explains how carbon forms four equivalent tetrahedral bonds. What explains why it does so?

choices.text: Hybrid orbitals overlap better and so form stronger bonds
Hybridization lets carbon hold more than eight electrons
choices.why: Carbon keeps an octet; the advantage is stronger bonding.

choices.text: Hybrid orbitals are spherical
choices.why: Hybrid orbitals are unsymmetrical, with one large lobe, which is why they bond well.

choices.text: The tetrahedral angle is required by the octet rule
choices.why: The octet rule counts electrons; the reason for hybridizing is stronger bonds.

explanation: The shape of the hybrid orbital suggests the answer to why: one lobe of an sp3 hybrid is larger and overlaps more effectively, so hybrid orbitals form stronger bonds than unhybridized s or p orbitals.

prompt: Which statement describes the shape of an sp3 hybrid orbital?

choices.text: It has two lobes of unequal size, so it points strongly in one direction
It is a sphere centered on the nucleus
choices.why: That is an s orbital. sp3 hybrids are unsymmetrical about the nucleus.

choices.text: It has two equal lobes, like a p orbital
choices.why: Mixing in the s orbital makes one lobe bigger than the other.

choices.text: It has four lobes, one for each bond
choices.why: Each sp3 hybrid has two lobes; carbon has four separate sp3 orbitals, one per bond.

explanation: The sp3 hybrids have two lobes and are unsymmetrical about the nucleus, giving them a directionality that lets them form strong bonds to other atoms.
